title: Gentiles as Gentiles: The Council in Jerusalem
sum: Teachers from Judea tell the believers at Antioch that Gentiles cannot be saved unless they are circumcised as the law of Moses requires. Paul and Barnabas oppose them, and the church sends them to Jerusalem. There believing Pharisees make the same demand. After long debate Peter recalls how God gave the Spirit to Cornelius' household without any distinction; Barnabas and Paul tell of signs among the Gentiles; and James, the Lord's brother, quotes Amos: God will rebuild David's fallen tent so that the nations may seek the Lord.

James rules that Gentile believers must not be burdened with circumcision and the whole law, but should keep away from four things: the pollution of idols, sexual sin, what is strangled and blood. A letter carried by Judas and Silas brings the decision to Antioch, where it is received with joy. The chapter ends with a quarrel: Paul and Barnabas split over John Mark, and Paul sets out with Silas. This is the hinge of Acts. From here on, the story follows Paul to the ends of the earth.
readings: Most historians accept that a meeting in Jerusalem settled, at least for a time, that Gentile believers did not have to be circumcised. Paul's letter to the Galatians tells of a meeting with James, Peter and John that agreed on this (Galatians 2:1–10), though it does not mention the four rules. Whether Galatians 2 describes this meeting or an earlier one, and whether the decree came at this meeting or later, is debated (see the note on 15:2).

Luke places the council at the exact center of Acts and tells it as the moment the church, guided by the Spirit and Scripture, opened its doors to the nations without asking them to become Jews. Every main character of the first half speaks: Peter for the last time, then Barnabas and Paul, then James, whose ruling unites the Jerusalem church and the Gentile mission. Unity, not victory, is the point: the letter is received with joy.

The debate is a Jewish one: how Gentiles who turn to Israel's God should relate to the Torah. James answers from the prophets and the laws for resident foreigners in Leviticus 17–18. Jewish scholars note that the council did not abolish the law for Jews: it set terms for Gentiles living among Jewish believers, close to the later rabbinic idea that righteous Gentiles keep the commandments given to Noah, not the whole law.

views.H: The council probably met around AD 48–49, after the first journey (Acts 13–14) and before Paul reached Corinth (AD 50–51). James the Lord's brother led the Jerusalem church until his death in AD 62 (Josephus, Antiquities 20.200). Syria and Cilicia formed a single Roman province governed from Antioch. Pressure on Jewish believers in Judea to keep clear of Gentiles may have grown in these years of rising nationalism under the Roman governors.
views.C: The relation of this chapter to Galatians 2 is the central problem: the same meeting, the earlier famine visit (11:30), or two meetings blended. Paul's letters never cite the decree, even where they discuss idol food (1 Corinthians 8–10), and 21:25 has James inform Paul of it as if it were news; so some scholars think the decree was issued later, without Paul. The speeches of Peter and James are widely seen as Luke's compositions, and James' use of the Septuagint of Amos is one argument for that. Others defend their substance (Bauckham, Witherington).
views.L: Acts 15 sits at the center of the book and echoes the Cornelius story (10–11), which Peter retells. The structure is a church meeting: dispute, testimony from experience, testimony of signs, proof from Scripture, decision, letter, joy. The phrase "it seemed good" runs through it (15:22, 25, 28), and the Spirit's part is stressed. The split of Paul and Barnabas immediately after the decree keeps the story honest: the church agrees on the gospel and still quarrels about people.
views.J: James' ruling resembles the laws for the resident foreigner (Leviticus 17–18), the clearest Torah model for non-Jews living among Israel. It anticipates the rabbinic teaching that Gentiles are bound by the commandments of Noah (Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 56a–b) and may be righteous without converting. Paula Fredriksen and others read the council as a Jewish movement deciding that, in the messianic age, the nations join Israel's God as nations, as Isaiah and Zechariah foresaw, rather than as converts.
views.T: The churches have long seen this meeting as the first council and the model for later ones: later councils echoed its decree language, "it seemed good ...," and some named the Holy Spirit as Acts does. Catholic and Orthodox teaching takes it as a pattern of apostolic authority exercised together; Protestants stress that the council judged by Scripture (James' appeal to Amos) and the evidence of God's work. The food rules were kept by many churches for centuries; the Orthodox Church still forbids eating blood.

deep.b:
For a Jewish man, circumcision was the sign of the covenant God made with Abraham, to be kept "generation after generation" (Genesis 17:12). For a Gentile man, it was the step that made him a Jew: Josephus tells of the royal house of Adiabene and of others who were circumcised to join Israel. Greeks and Romans found it odd and even shameful. So the demand of the Judean teachers was not only about a ritual. It asked whether Gentile believers had to become Jews, with all that meant for their families and cities, in order to belong to Israel's Messiah.

The apostles' answer was no, and their reasons are given in order: God gave these Gentiles the Spirit without circumcision (15:8); he made no distinction, cleansing their hearts by faith (15:9); salvation for Jews and Gentiles alike comes through the grace of the Lord Jesus (15:11); and the prophets foresaw the nations belonging to the Lord as nations (15:16–17). The four rules that follow are not a lighter path to salvation but the conditions for living together as one people.

James' proof text comes from the last chapter of Amos. In the Hebrew, Amos promises that the fallen booth of David will be rebuilt so that Israel may take possession of what is left of Edom and of all the nations over whom the LORD's name has been called (Amos 9:12). The Greek translation known in Luke's day reads "so that the rest of humankind may seek out" the Lord. James' words follow the Greek closely, with an opening echo of Jeremiah 12:15 and a close echo of Isaiah 45:21.

Richard Bauckham has argued that the quotation is a careful Jewish interpretation, combining several prophets in the way Jewish teachers did, and that its point stands even in the Hebrew: the nations over whom the LORD's name has been called belong to the LORD without becoming Israelites. Others think Luke himself composed the speech from the Septuagint. Either way, the church's decision is presented as Scripture read in the light of what God had done.

deep.title: Claude's theory: three witnesses
deep.b: The law of Moses says, "A matter is to stand on the word of two witnesses or on the word of three witnesses" (Deuteronomy 19:15). The council hears exactly three kinds of testimony: Peter tells what God did through the Spirit (15:7–11), Barnabas and Paul tell of signs and wonders (15:12), and James brings the witness of the prophets (15:15–18). Only then does James give judgment: "my decision is this" (15:19; literally "I judge"). My suggestion is that Luke shaped the scene as a Jewish court reaching a verdict on three testimonies, so that Jewish-Christian readers would see the decision as lawful by the Torah's own rules. Commentators such as Luke Timothy Johnson note the threefold argument from experience, signs and Scripture; the link to the rule of witnesses is my own guess, and Luke does not make it explicit.

echoes: Genesis 17:9–14; Leviticus 17:7–15; Leviticus 18:6–26; Amos 9:11–12; Jeremiah 12:15; Isaiah 45:21; Zechariah 2:11; Deuteronomy 28:10; 10:1–11:18; 13:1–14:28; 16:4; 21:18–26; Galatians 2:1–14; 1 Corinthians 8:1–13; Revelation 2:14; Revelation 2:20

settings.what: The demand that Gentile believers be circumcised
settings.by: Some believers who came down from Judea
settings.to: The church at Antioch, a mixed body of Jewish and Gentile believers
settings.when: After Paul and Barnabas returned from their first journey (14:26–28), probably around AD 48
settings.why: To bring the Gentile believers fully under the covenant of Abraham and the law of Moses, which these teachers took to be the only way to belong to Israel's Messiah. They spoke as Jews loyal to Genesis 17, and their demand threatened the shared life of the church at Antioch, where Jews and Gentiles ate together.
settings.readers: Luke's mostly Gentile readers knew the question had been answered, but they needed to know how: not by setting the law aside lightly, but by the apostles, the Spirit and Scripture together.
views: Galatians 2:12 speaks of "certain men from James" whose arrival made Peter stop eating with Gentiles. Some link them with these visitors; 15:24 says the apostles had given them no instructions.
Others think these were believers from a strict party in Judea acting on their own, like the Pharisee believers of 15:5.

settings.by: Believers from the party of the Pharisees
settings.to: The apostles, elders and church in Jerusalem, as Paul and Barnabas report on their mission
settings.when: At the reception of the delegation from Antioch
settings.why: To insist that Gentile converts be circumcised and told to keep the Torah. As Pharisees they cared for exact observance; as believers they assumed that Israel's Messiah gathered his people under Israel's law.
settings.readers: Luke shows that the opposition came from inside the church and was argued in good faith, which made the apostles' answer all the more weighty.

settings.to: The apostles and elders in Jerusalem, with the gathered church (15:12, 22)
settings.when: After long debate at the council
settings.why: To settle the matter by pointing to what God had already done: the Spirit given to Cornelius' Gentile household (10:44–48), hearts cleansed by faith, and salvation by the grace of the Lord Jesus for Jews and Gentiles alike. Peter speaks as the apostle God first sent to Gentiles, and warns that adding the law's yoke would be testing God.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers this is the last word of Peter in Acts, and it hands the story over to Paul. Its message, that Jews are saved in the same way as Gentiles, sums up what Luke's Gentile readers needed to know about their place in God's people.

settings.what: Barnabas and Paul's report to the council
settings.to: The whole gathering of apostles, elders and church in Jerusalem
settings.when: After Peter's speech, when the meeting had gone quiet
settings.why: To add to Peter's witness the evidence of the first journey: the signs and wonders God had worked among Gentiles through them (13–14). The point was that God himself had already accepted uncircumcised Gentiles and confirmed it with his works.
settings.readers: Luke gives only a one-line summary, since his readers had just read the journey in chapters 13–14. Barnabas is named first, as the Jerusalem church knew him best (see the note).

settings.by: James, the brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem church
settings.to: The council of apostles and elders and the Jerusalem church
settings.when: After the testimony of Peter, Barnabas and Paul
settings.why: To show from the prophets (Amos 9:11–12) that God always meant to gather a people from the nations, and to propose a practical ruling: no circumcision for Gentile believers, but four rules drawn from the Torah's laws for foreigners living among Israel, so that Jewish and Gentile believers could live together and Jews in every synagogue would not be offended. Coming from James, known for his loyalty to the law, the ruling could carry the Jerusalem church.
settings.readers: Luke's readers learned that their freedom from circumcision was not a break with Scripture but its fulfillment, decided by the most law-observant leader of the church.
views: Bauckham argues that the speech reflects a skilled Jewish reading of the prophets that James could have made.
Many critics think Luke wrote the speech, since it depends on the Greek wording of Amos.

settings.by: The apostles and elders in Jerusalem, with the whole church
settings.to: Gentile believers in Antioch and the province of Syria and Cilicia
settings.when: Sent with Judas and Silas, together with Paul and Barnabas, after the council
settings.why: To undo the damage done by the Judean teachers, to state that circumcision and the whole law would not be laid on Gentile believers, and to bind them to four "necessary things": no food sacrificed to idols, no blood, no meat from strangled animals, no sexual sin. As law, it bound Gentile believers in the churches, not Jews (who kept the Torah) and not outsiders. It settled the Gentiles' standing and set terms on which Jewish and Gentile believers could share one church; whether its rules were meant above all for shared tables, or as the Torah's laws for foreigners living among Israel, is debated (see the note on 15:20).
settings.readers: Luke's readers, perhaps a generation later, could see where their church's food customs came from, and that they rested on a decision of the Spirit and the apostles rather than on the law of Moses as such.
views: Luke has Paul deliver the decree to the churches of the first journey (16:4) and James recall it later (21:25).
Others note the letter's address to Antioch, Syria and Cilicia only, and Paul's silence about it, and see it as a local settlement later applied more widely.

settings.what: Paul's proposal to revisit the churches
settings.when: Some days after the delegation's return
settings.why: To check on the churches founded on the first journey and strengthen them, now with the council's decision in hand. The plan led to the quarrel over Mark and so to two missions instead of one.
settings.readers: Luke's readers saw that even leaders filled with the Spirit could part in anger, and that God used the split.

traditions.q: What authority does a church council have (15:6–29)?
views: The college of bishops, in union with the pope, exercises supreme authority over the whole church in an ecumenical council, and its definitions on faith and morals are infallible. Acts 15 is the pattern: the apostles and elders meeting together and saying, "it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us" (Catechism 884, 891; Lumen Gentium 22, 25).

The Holy Spirit guides the church through councils of bishops, and the seven ecumenical councils hold supreme authority in faith. Their decisions are recognized as true when the whole church receives them, as the church of Antioch received the apostles' letter with joy (15:31); the Encyclical of the Eastern Patriarchs (1848) says that the guardian of the faith is the whole body of the church, the people themselves.

Councils have authority to teach only what Scripture teaches; they can err and have erred. Luther argued that the council of Acts 15 did not create new articles of faith but defended the old one, that we are saved by grace (15:11).

General councils "may err, and sometimes have erred, even in things pertaining unto God," and what they order as necessary to salvation has authority only if it can be shown from Scripture (Article 21). In practice Anglicans have received the creeds and the first four general councils as faithful to Scripture.

Synods and councils may be held for the better government of the church and may decide controversies of faith, so far as their decrees agree with the Word of God. But all councils since the apostles may err, so they are not to be made the rule of faith (Westminster Confession 31). Presbyterian church government, with elders meeting in higher assemblies, appeals to Acts 15.

Each local church is self-governing under Christ. Churches may meet by their messengers to consult on hard questions, but such assemblies hold no power over the churches (Second London Confession 26.15). Acts 15 shows churches seeking common counsel, not a higher court.

title: Across to Europe: Timothy, Lydia and the Jailer
sum: Paul returns to Derbe and Lystra, where he finds Timothy, a young believer with a Jewish mother and a Greek father, and circumcises him to take him along. The churches receive the Jerusalem decrees and grow. Then every way forward seems blocked: the Holy Spirit stops them from preaching in Asia, and the Spirit of Jesus will not let them enter Bithynia. At Troas Paul sees a vision of a man of Macedonia calling for help, and here the story switches to "we."

At Philippi, a Roman colony, the first believer in Europe is Lydia, a seller of purple cloth who worships God, baptized with her household. A slave girl with a Python spirit follows them shouting, until Paul drives the spirit out; her masters drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, who have them beaten and jailed. At midnight, as they pray and sing, an earthquake opens the prison. Paul stops the jailer from killing himself, and the jailer and his household believe and are baptized. In the morning Paul reveals that he and Silas are Roman citizens and demands that the magistrates come and release them in person.
readings: The chapter is full of precise detail: the route through Samothrace and Neapolis, Philippi's status as a colony, its magistrates and rod-bearers, the place of prayer by the river. With the first "we" (16:10), many readers believe the author himself is now traveling with Paul. Historians regard the founding of the church at Philippi as secure; Paul's letter to the Philippians and his mention of mistreatment there (1 Thessalonians 2:2) confirm the outline.
Read as a story of the gospel and Rome

Luke tells of three people across the social ladder touched by the gospel: a wealthy merchant woman, a slave girl delivered from a spirit, and a Roman jailer. Two of them believe; of the girl Luke tells only her deliverance. The charge against Paul is that his customs are not fit for Romans; the outcome is that the magistrates have broken Roman law against Roman citizens. Luke's readers are being told that the gospel is no threat to good order, and that Rome's own law protected its messengers.

views.H: Philippi had been a Roman colony since 42 BC, settled with veterans after the battle against Brutus and Cassius; its two chief magistrates were attended by lictors with rods. Paul probably arrived around AD 49–50. Jews were few there, and Claudius' expulsion of Jews from Rome about this time (18:2) may explain the charge "They are Jews." The Via Egnatia led on from Philippi to Thessalonica.
views.C: The "we" passage that begins at 16:10 raises the question of the author's presence (see the note there). Timothy's circumcision sits uneasily with Galatians 2:3 and 5:2, and critics such as Haenchen doubt it. The prison miracle shares motifs with Greek stories, especially Euripides' Bacchae; some scholars think Luke built the scene on such models, while others accept a real earthquake and a release. Paul's late claim to citizenship has also been questioned, though no one doubts that Paul was beaten at Philippi.
views.L: The Spirit's guidance shapes the chapter: twice forbidden, then a vision, then "we" sure that God had called. Salvation words ring through it: the slave girl announces "a way to be saved" (16:17), the jailer asks "what do I have to do to be saved?" (16:30), and the answer comes, "you will be saved" (16:31). Two households, Lydia's and the jailer's, frame the stay in Philippi, and the story ends where it began, in Lydia's home.
views.J: Paul begins, as always, with Jews and God-worshipers at a place of prayer on the Sabbath. Timothy's circumcision shows Paul honoring Jewish identity even as he carries the decree that frees Gentiles from circumcision; scholars who read Paul "within Judaism" (Fredriksen, Nanos) find this consistent. The Philippian accusers use anti-Jewish prejudice against the missionaries, a reminder of how vulnerable Jewish communities were in Roman cities.
views.T: The household baptisms of Lydia and the jailer are a classic text in the debate over infant baptism. The jailer's question, "what do I have to do to be saved?" and Paul's answer have been the text of countless evangelistic sermons. The church fathers praised the singing in prison as a model of joy in suffering, and the Orthodox and Catholic calendars honor Lydia as the first convert in Europe.

deep.b:
Luke's account of Philippi is built around three people. Lydia was a businesswoman from Thyatira in Asia, dealing in costly purple cloth, the head of her own household, and a Gentile worshiper of Israel's God. The slave girl was at the bottom of the social order, owned by several masters who made money from her oracles; Luke tells of her deliverance but not of her faith, and she disappears from the story. The jailer was probably a public slave or a minor official of the colony, a man responsible with his life for his prisoners.

Together they show the reach of the gospel in a Roman colony: a free woman of means, a slave, and a servant of Roman power. Paul's letter to this church, written years later from prison, is the warmest of his letters. He thanks them for their partnership "from the first day" (Philippians 1:5) and for gifts they sent more than once, and he names women, Euodia and Syntyche, who worked hard beside him.

deep.h: Did Paul contradict himself over Timothy?
deep.b:
Paul had just carried a decree saying that Gentile believers need not be circumcised, and in Galatians he refused to have Titus circumcised (Galatians 2:3). Here he circumcises Timothy. The usual answer turns on two facts. First, Timothy's mother was Jewish, so to Jews he was either a Jew who had not been circumcised or someone who ought to have been; Paul's opponents later accused him of teaching Jews not to circumcise their sons (21:21), and Timothy's case would answer that. Second, Paul's principle was that circumcision does not save (Galatians 5:6; 1 Corinthians 7:19), not that Jews must stop practicing it.

Critical scholars reply that Luke's Paul is more law-observant than the Paul of the letters, and that the story may reflect Luke's concern to show Paul as a loyal Jew. Shaye Cohen has questioned whether Timothy would have been counted a Jew at all in the first century. The episode remains one of the test cases for how far Acts and Paul's letters agree.

deep.title: Claude's theory: who are the Romans?
deep.b: The slave girl's owners accuse Paul and Silas as outsiders: "They are Jews," teaching customs that "we, as Romans" may not follow (16:20–21). Paul's reply the next morning turns the same words back: "We are Romans" (16:37). The men accused of being un-Roman were citizens, and the magistrates who claimed to defend Roman ways had broken Roman law. My suggestion is that Luke arranged the scene around this echo on purpose, so that "Romans" frames the Philippian story from charge to vindication, and that it speaks to Luke's readers, who may have faced the same accusation of following un-Roman customs. Commentators note the irony of the citizenship scene; the deliberate pairing of 16:21 and 16:37 as a frame is my own reading.

echoes: Genesis 14:18–20; Genesis 17:7; Psalm 119:62; 1 Samuel 28:7; Galatians 2:3; Galatians 5:2–6; 1 Corinthians 9:19–23; 2 Timothy 1:5; 10:1–48; 11:14; 12:6–11; 5:17–25; 22:25–29; Philippians 1:1–11; Philippians 4:2–3; 1 Thessalonians 2:2; 2 Corinthians 11:25

settings.what: The Macedonian's call in a vision
settings.by: A man of Macedonia, seen in a night vision
settings.when: After the Spirit had twice blocked the way, in Asia and in Bithynia
settings.why: To redirect the mission across the sea to Macedonia: "Cross over ... and help us." Paul and his companions took it as God's call to bring the good news to Europe.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, many of them in the Greek cities, this was the moment the gospel came to their part of the world, by God's direction rather than by human planning.

settings.to: Paul and his companions, including the narrator ("us")
settings.when: Right after her household was baptized
settings.why: To show her faith by hospitality, and to make her home the base of the mission. Her words, "If you have decided that I am a true believer," ask the missionaries to treat a Gentile woman's household as fit company.
settings.readers: Luke's readers, who met in houses, would recognize the beginning of a house church and the importance of women of means in the first churches.

settings.by: A slave girl with a Python spirit
settings.to: The people of Philippi on the road to the place of prayer, about Paul and his companions
settings.when: Day after day, as the missionaries went to the place of prayer
settings.why: On the surface, to announce the missionaries; underneath, the spirit's words could tie their message to the oracle trade and confuse "the Most High God" with pagan gods. Paul silenced it rather than accept its help.
settings.readers: Luke's readers learned that true words from a false source were not to be welcomed, and that Jesus' name was stronger than the spirits of the Greek oracles.

settings.to: The spirit in the slave girl
settings.when: After many days of her shouting
settings.why: To drive out the spirit by the authority of Jesus' name, freeing the girl and ending the confusion her cries caused.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers the scene matched Jesus' own exorcisms in the Gospel and showed the risen Lord at work through his apostles.

settings.to: The two magistrates of the colony, in the marketplace with a crowd
settings.when: Immediately after the exorcism ended their income
settings.why: To get rid of the men who had cost them money, by turning a private loss into a public charge: these Jews were disturbing the city and teaching customs unlawful for Romans. The charge played on prejudice against Jews and on Roman fear of foreign cults.
settings.readers: Luke's readers could see that the charge was false and the motive greed, a pattern repeated at Ephesus (19:23–27).

settings.what: The jailer's question and the answer
settings.by: The jailer, then Paul and Silas
settings.to: Paul and Silas; then the jailer and his household
settings.when: At midnight, after the earthquake, as the jailer was about to kill himself
settings.why: Paul's shout saved the jailer's life; the jailer's question, "what do I have to do to be saved?" asked for rescue, and Paul and Silas answered with the gospel, offering salvation to him and his household through faith in the Lord Jesus.
settings.readers: Luke's readers heard in this exchange the simplest form of the gospel offer, made to a servant of Rome in the middle of the night.

settings.what: The release order and Paul's protest
settings.by: The magistrates, through their rod-bearers; then Paul
settings.to: The jailer and Paul; then the rod-bearers and, through them, the magistrates
settings.why: The magistrates wanted the trouble to disappear quietly. Paul, a Roman citizen beaten without trial, refused to slip away and demanded a public release, probably to protect the young church at Philippi from suspicion once he had gone.
settings.readers: Luke's readers learned that Christians could appeal to Roman law, and that Roman officials themselves had to admit Paul's innocence.

traditions.q: Did the household baptisms (16:15, 33) include infants?
views: Infant baptism is an immemorial tradition of the church, and it is quite possible that infants were baptized from the beginning, when whole households received baptism, as at Philippi (Catechism 1252).

A household entered the church together, and the Orthodox read Lydia's and the jailer's households that way: the faith of the head of the house brought all its members, children included, to baptism, as infants are still baptized, chrismated and given communion.

Infants are baptized because of God's command and promise, not because these texts prove it (Large Catechism, on Baptism). On the households themselves Lutheran scholars are divided: Joachim Jeremias argued that the biblical "household" formula took in small children, and Kurt Aland replied that the texts cannot show any infants were present.

The household baptisms continue the pattern of Abraham, whose whole household received the covenant sign with him (Genesis 17:23). The promise "you and your household" (16:31) is covenant language, so the infants of believers are to be baptized (Westminster Confession 28.4).

Only those who profess repentance and faith are proper subjects of baptism (Second London Confession 29.2). At Philippi the word was spoken to all in the jailer's house, and the whole household believed and rejoiced (16:32, 34), so the text does not show infants being baptized.

The household texts say nothing of infants, and baptism is for those who have learned repentance and ask for it themselves (Schleitheim Confession, article 1); a household is baptized when each member believes.

title: Another King and an Unknown God
sum: In Thessalonica Paul argues from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths that the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and that Jesus is the Messiah. Some Jews, many God-worshiping Greeks and leading women believe. Jealous opponents raise a mob, drag Jason before the city rulers and accuse the believers of defying Caesar by calling Jesus king. Paul and Silas escape by night to Berea, where the Jews eagerly examine the Scriptures and many believe, until agitators arrive and Paul is sent on to Athens.

In Athens, a city full of idols, Paul argues in the synagogue and the marketplace and is brought to the Areopagus by Epicurean and Stoic philosophers. His speech starts from an altar "To an unknown god" and proclaims the Creator, who needs nothing from human hands, made all nations from one, and is near to everyone. Quoting a Greek poet, "we are his offspring," he argues against idols, calls all people to repent, and announces a day of judgment by a man whom God raised from the dead. Some mock, some want to hear more, and a few believe, among them Dionysius of the Areopagus and a woman named Damaris.
readings: Read as a model of preaching to outsiders

The Areopagus speech is the New Testament's fullest example of the gospel addressed to educated pagans. Paul finds common ground with his hearers (their altars, their poets, their philosophers' belief in a God who needs nothing), and then moves beyond it to repentance, judgment and resurrection. Missionaries and apologists have studied it as a pattern for speaking to cultures without the Bible.

Many scholars, following Martin Dibelius, see the speech as Luke's own model sermon, Greek in its themes and polished in its style, placed at the cultural capital of the Greek world. Others, such as F. F. Bruce, argue that it fits what Paul says in Romans 1 and 1 Thessalonians 1:9–10 and could summarize what Paul actually said.
Read with the letters to Thessalonica

Probably Paul's first surviving letter (unless Galatians is earlier) was written to the church founded in this chapter, only months later. It recalls how the Thessalonians turned from idols to serve God and wait for his Son from heaven (1 Thessalonians 1:9–10), how they suffered from their own people (2:14), and how Paul longed to return. Acts and the letter differ on details, such as Timothy's movements, but agree on the main lines.

views.H: Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a free city whose officials were called politarchs, a title confirmed by inscriptions. Berea lay about fifty miles west. Athens in the 50s was no longer a great power but remained the center of Greek philosophy and art, governed by its old council of the Areopagus, with authority in religious matters. The altars "to unknown gods" are mentioned by Pausanias and Philostratus.
views.C: Whether the Areopagus speech is Paul's or Luke's has been debated since Dibelius (1939). Vielhauer argued that its natural theology does not fit the Paul of Romans 1, where knowledge of God leaves people without excuse; others answer that Romans 1:19–21 and the speech say much the same. Acts' report that Paul stayed only three Sabbaths in Thessalonica, and its account of Silas and Timothy, differ from hints in 1 Thessalonians and Philippians.
views.L: The chapter moves from synagogue to marketplace to the Areopagus, from Scripture-based argument to philosophy, and from a charge of "another king" to a proclamation of the world's judge. The pattern of Acts repeats twice (preaching, belief, jealousy, flight), then breaks at Athens, where there is mockery but no riot. The speech ends where Paul's preaching always ends in Acts: with Jesus raised from the dead.
views.J: Paul begins in the synagogues, arguing from the Jewish Scriptures; the Bereans are praised as model Jews who test his message by those Scriptures. The opposition in Thessalonica comes from Jews who saw their God-fearing patrons drawn away. The Areopagus speech uses the Jewish case against idols (Isaiah 40–46; Wisdom of Solomon 13–15) and Jewish monotheism, presented in Greek terms as Hellenistic Jewish writers like Aristobulus and Philo had done.
views.T: The speech has been a key text for natural theology, the knowledge of God available through creation and reason, which Catholic teaching affirms and some Protestant theologians, especially Karl Barth, reject. Dionysius the Areopagite became, in tradition, the first bishop of Athens, and writings under his name around AD 500 shaped Christian mysticism East and West. The Bereans became a byword for searching the Scriptures.

deep.h: The Areopagus speech step by step
deep.b:
Opening (17:22–23). Paul praises the Athenians' devotion and seizes on an altar "To an unknown god": what they revere without knowing, he will make known.

God the Creator (17:24–25). The maker of the world, Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in handmade shrines or need human service; he gives life and breath to all. Isaiah 42:5 and 1 Kings 8:27 stand behind this, but Stoics could agree.

God and humankind (17:26–28). From one ancestor God made every nation, fixed their times and places, so that they would seek him; he is near to each one. Paul quotes a Greek poet: "For we are his offspring too."

Against idols (17:29). If we are God's offspring, God cannot be like gold, silver or stone.

The call (17:30–31). God overlooked the times of ignorance but now commands all people to repent, because he has set a day to judge the world through a man he appointed and raised from the dead.

The movement is from what the hearers already believe to what they do not: from creation to judgment, from the altar of an unknown god to the man God raised. The speech never names Jesus, but the resurrection, which the Athenians had heard Paul preach (17:18), is its last word.

Paul quotes Greek literature three times in the New Testament: Aratus here, Menander in 1 Corinthians 15:33 (on bad company and good character), and, according to Clement of Alexandria and others, Epimenides in Titus 1:12. The line from Aratus, a poet from Cilicia like Paul, had already been used by the Jewish writer Aristobulus to speak of the one God. Christians have argued since then about how much truth pagan literature contains. Justin Martyr spoke of "seeds of the Word" scattered among the Greeks; Tertullian asked what Athens had to do with Jerusalem. Paul's use here is selective: he takes a true insight, that humans are God's kin, and turns it against the idols that the poet's own religion made.

deep.title: Claude's theory: resurrection on the hill of the court
deep.b: According to Athenian legend, told in Aeschylus' play The Eumenides, the court of the Areopagus was founded by Athena to try Orestes. In that trial the god Apollo declares that once a man has died and the dust has drunk his blood, there is no anastasis, no rising again. Every educated Athenian knew the play. Luke has Paul announce anastasis before that same court, and some of his hearers sneer at exactly that word (17:32). My suggestion is that Luke, who knew Greek literature, chose to end the speech on the resurrection partly because it struck at a saying linked to the founding of the Areopagus itself. Some commentators cite the Aeschylus line as background; the claim that Luke intended the contrast is my own and cannot be proved.

echoes: Genesis 1:26–28; Genesis 2:7; Genesis 10:32; Deuteronomy 4:29; Deuteronomy 32:8; 1 Kings 8:27; Psalm 9:8; Psalm 50:9–12; Psalm 96:13; Isaiah 40:18–20; Isaiah 42:5; Isaiah 44:9–20; Isaiah 55:6; Isaiah 66:1–2; Daniel 7:13–14; 14:15–17; Luke 23:2; Luke 24:25–27; Romans 1:18–25; 1 Thessalonians 1:9–10; 1 Thessalonians 2:1–3:6

settings.what: Paul's arguments in the synagogue at Thessalonica
settings.to: The Jews of the Thessalonica synagogue, with God-worshiping Greeks and leading women
settings.when: On three Sabbaths, after his arrival from Philippi
settings.why: To show from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead, and that Jesus is that Messiah. For Jews who expected a victorious Messiah, a crucified one had to be proved from Scripture before anything else.
settings.readers: Luke's readers were shown the shape of the apostles' preaching to Jews, the same argument the risen Jesus made on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:25–27).

settings.what: The charge before the city rulers
settings.to: The politarchs of Thessalonica, with a crowd
settings.when: When the mob failed to find Paul and Silas at Jason's house
settings.why: To get the missionaries and their host punished by accusing them of sedition: upsetting the empire, defying Caesar's decrees, proclaiming another king. In a city that owed much to Rome's favor, such a charge was dangerous.
settings.readers: Luke's readers, who might face the same charge, were shown that it was a distortion: Jesus is king, but his followers were no rebels, and the city rulers merely took a bond.

settings.to: Jews and God-worshiping Gentiles in the synagogue, and whoever happened by in the marketplace (the agora)
settings.when: Day by day while he waited in Athens for Silas and Timothy
settings.why: Stirred by the city's idols (17:16), Paul argued for the gospel in both of the city's meeting places: in the synagogue with those who knew the Scriptures, and in the agora with anyone at all, in the open way Athenian teachers since Socrates had argued with passers-by.
settings.readers: Luke's readers saw Paul at home among Jews and in the most famous public square of Greek learning, which leads into the philosophers' challenge and the speech.

settings.to: Paul, in the marketplace and then at the Areopagus
settings.when: After days of Paul's debates in the Athenian marketplace
settings.why: Partly mockery ("this seed-picker"), partly curiosity about a teaching that sounded like foreign gods. Bringing him to the Areopagus may have been an official inquiry into a new teacher, or simply a hearing.
settings.readers: Luke's readers saw the gospel taken seriously enough to be heard before Athens' ancient court, in the city of Socrates.

settings.to: The Athenians gathered at the Areopagus, perhaps the council itself, including Epicurean and Stoic philosophers
settings.when: During Paul's stay in Athens while he waited for Silas and Timothy, probably about AD 50
settings.why: To introduce educated pagans to the God of Israel without assuming they knew the Scriptures: starting from their own altar and poets, Paul presents the Creator who needs nothing, shows the folly of idols, and calls them to repent before the day of judgment, proven by the resurrection of the appointed man. Knowing the hearers explains the speech's style: no Old Testament quotations, no name of Jesus, philosophical language, and a sharp turn at the end.
settings.readers: Luke's mostly Gentile readers, many of them converts from paganism, could hear their own story: turning from idols to the living God and waiting for his judgment and the risen one.
views: Bruce and Witherington think it summarizes a real address, matching Paul's teaching in Romans 1 and 1 Thessalonians 1:9–10.
Dibelius and many critics consider it Luke's model sermon to Gentiles, written in a Greek philosophical style.

traditions.q: Can people know God from nature and reason, without Scripture (17:22–31)?
views: Yes: God, the beginning and end of all things, can be known with certainty from created things by the natural light of human reason, though revelation is needed to know him fully and for salvation (First Vatican Council, Dei Filius 2; Catechism 36).

God makes himself known through creation and conscience, and every person has a longing for him; yet God's essence is beyond all knowing, and true knowledge of him comes by his self-revelation and by communion with him, not by reasoning alone.

God has planted an awareness of himself in every human mind and shows himself in his works, but sin turns this knowledge into idolatry, so it leaves people without excuse but cannot save them; Scripture is needed as spectacles to see God rightly (Calvin, Institutes 1.3–6). In the twentieth century Karl Barth rejected natural theology altogether.

There is a twofold knowledge of God: a general one, that God exists, made the world and punishes evil, which all people have; and a particular one, what God thinks of us and wills to do for us in Christ, which comes only through the gospel (Luther, Lectures on Galatians, on 4:8). Natural knowledge cannot reach God's grace.
